chunks: From him, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the 'farah' (a type of cattle, specifically a cow or ox). I said: 'I buy it from a man whom I do not fully trust, and he sells it to me on the basis that it is 'thakiyyah' (sound/healthy). Should I sell it on that basis?' He said: 'If you do not trust him, do not sell it on the basis that it is 'thakiyyah', unless you say: "It has been said to me that it is sound."'

key_terms.أَبَا عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdillah, referring to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him).
key_terms.الْغَرَرِ: Uncertainty or ambiguity in a contract.
key_terms.الْفِرَاءِ: A type of cattle, specifically a cow or ox.

ai.seo_question: How to handle selling livestock when the buyer does not trust the seller's claim of health?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the practical application of avoiding *gharar* (uncertainty) in commercial transactions by distinguishing between a definitive guarantee and a reported claim. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) advises using the phrase 'it has been said to me' to shift the burden of verification, thereby protecting the buyer from liability if the animal proves defective. This reflects the Shia juristic principle of prioritizing caution in dealings with untrusted parties to preserve contractual validity.
